note: Yoḥanan ben Narbbai and his household were said to eat three hundred calves, drink three hundred jugs of wine and eat forty se'a of doves for dessert, so that in his days no sacrificial meat was ever left over. As for Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai: a king and queen argued whether goat or lamb is better and asked the High Priest. Yissakhar waved his hand in contempt and said that if goat were better, it would be the daily offering. The king, angered at his lack of respect, ordered his right hand cut off. Yissakhar bribed the official, who cut off his left; when the king heard, he had the right cut off too. Rav Yosef blessed God for punishing Yissakhar in this world.
why: The Gemara has listed the cries raised in the Temple courtyard against unworthy priests and for worthy ones, including Yissakhar and Yoḥanan ben Narbbai; this tells what each man was like and how Yissakhar ended.

note: Rav Huna son of Rav Natan visited the house of Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak. Asked his name, he said 'Rav Huna', title and all. Invited to sit on the couch, he sat at once; offered a cup, he took it the first time, drank it in two sips, and did not turn his face away. His hosts asked about each act. He said he had always been called by that name; that a guest does whatever the host says, except leave; that one may refuse a lesser person but not a great one; that drinking a cup in one gulp is greedy, in two is good manners and in three is haughty; and that only a bride turns her face.
why: The mishna says that a bride eating the Passover offering with a group turns her face away, out of embarrassment; Rav Huna cites that rule to explain why he, not being a bride, did not turn his.

note: When Rabbi Akiva was in prison, Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai asked him to teach him Torah, and Rabbi Akiva refused. Rabbi Shimon joked that he would tell his father Yoḥai to turn Rabbi Akiva over to the government. Rabbi Akiva answered that the cow wants to nurse even more than the calf wants to suck; Rabbi Shimon replied that it is the calf that is in danger. Rabbi Akiva then gave him five teachings: if you would hang yourself, hang from a tall tree; teach your son from a corrected text; do not cook in a pot your fellow cooked in; eating fruit without payment is a mitzva and good for the body; and marrying a wife is a mitzva that keeps the body pure and brings children.
why: The Gemara has just quoted seven pieces of advice Rabbi Akiva gave his son; it adds the five he gave Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, then moves on to similar instructions Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave his sons.
